questions.stem: An 11 month old boy has a large, tense swelling of his left thigh 2 days after his routine intramuscular vaccinations. He has bruises on his shins and knees since he began crawling. He is otherwise well. There are no other injuries. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A deep muscle haematoma after an IM injection in a young boy, with an isolated prolonged APTT and a very low factor VIII, is severe haemophilia A.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: large, tense swelling of his left thigh
steps.x: A male infant, a deep bleed into muscle after a minor injury, bruising as he starts to move.

elim: The platelet count is normal.
Bruises are on crawling sites, and the clotting screen and factor VIII explain them.
Would prolong the PT as well as the APTT.
Usually causes mucosal bleeding, and the deep muscle bleed with factor VIII of 2% fits haemophilia.

steps.x: **A. Haemophilia A.** Boy + deep bleeding + isolated long APTT + low factor VIII = haemophilia A.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has oozed blood from a wisdom tooth socket for 3 days. He had two swollen knees after falls as a child that were never investigated. His uncle on his mother's side bled heavily after surgery. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Prolonged APTT with normal PT, a normal factor VIII and a low factor IX is haemophilia B.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Post-procedure bleeding, past haemarthroses, a maternal uncle affected.

elim: Would prolong the PT, which is normal.
Factor VIII is normal, which excludes haemophilia A.
Would prolong the PT and lower several factors.
Factor VIII is normal, and he has deep joint bleeds rather than mucosal bleeding alone.

steps.x: **C. Haemophilia B.** Isolated long APTT + normal factor VIII + low factor IX = haemophilia B.

questions.stem: A 14 year old girl with Turner syndrome (45,X) has had heavy bleeding after a tooth extraction and a painful swollen knee after a minor fall. Her father has severe haemophilia A. Her APTT is 66 s (25–35) and PT 12 s (10–14).
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her bleeding?
o: Haemophilia A from a single affected X chromosome
Lyonisation in a carrier with two X chromosomes
Von Willebrand disease from her father
questions.e: Her only X came from her father, who has haemophilia A; with no second X to compensate, a Turner syndrome girl can be a symptomatic carrier.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: Her father has severe haemophilia A
steps.x: One X chromosome, inherited from an affected father; haemophilia-type bleeding.

elim: Rare in a child; her genetics explain it.
Causes a low platelet count and a normal APTT.
She has only one X chromosome (45,X).
Her father has haemophilia A, and haemarthrosis with a long APTT fits that.

steps.x: **B. Haemophilia A from a single affected X chromosome.** X-linked recessive: females are usually asymptomatic carriers, but 45,X means the single faulty X is expressed.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman attends clinic because her 2 year old son has just been diagnosed with severe haemophilia A. Her brother also has haemophilia A. She has never had abnormal bleeding, including after childbirth. Her partner is unaffected.
questions.q: Which best describes this woman?
o: Carrier of an autosomal dominant trait
questions.e: Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive: males are affected, and a woman with an affected son and brother is an obligate carrier, usually without symptoms.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: Her brother also has haemophilia A
steps.x: An affected son and brother, and no bleeding herself.

elim: Women are rarely affected because the normal X compensates; she has no bleeding.
Haemophilia is X-linked recessive.
Her family have haemophilia A, not von Willebrand disease.
With an affected son and an affected brother she is an obligate carrier.

steps.x: **B. Asymptomatic carrier.** X-linked recessive: males affected, females usually asymptomatic carriers.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy with severe haemophilia A has had 3 hours of pain and tingling in his right elbow after a fall onto it. The elbow is warm, swollen and held flexed, and he cannot straighten it. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. An X-ray shows no fracture.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Early tingling, then a warm, swollen joint with reduced movement after minor trauma in haemophilia is a bleed into the joint.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: pain and tingling in his right elbow
steps.x: Haemophilia, minor trauma, fast onset, a warm swollen joint held flexed, no fever.

elim: Very unusual at 16, and the trauma with haemophilia explains the joint.
A swelling behind the elbow that does not block movement of the joint.
Follows infection and is not triggered by a fall.
He is afebrile, and the onset follows trauma within hours.

steps.x: **A. Acute haemarthrosis.** Haemophilia + swollen painful joint after minor injury = haemarthrosis until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 21 year old man with severe haemophilia B has had pain in his right groin for 1 day after a long cycle ride. He keeps his right hip flexed and extension is very painful, but gentle rotation is pain free. He has numbness over the front of his right thigh. His temperature is 37.1°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A deep muscle bleed into iliopsoas holds the hip flexed, hurts on extension but spares rotation, and can compress the femoral nerve.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: extension is very painful, but gentle rotation is pain free
numbness over the front of his right thigh
steps.x: Haemophilia, a fixed flexed hip that rotates freely, femoral nerve numbness.

elim: Does not cause anterior thigh numbness or a fixed flexed hip with free rotation.
Presents as a groin lump, not a flexed hip with nerve symptoms.
A bleed into the joint itself makes rotation painful too.
He is afebrile, and rotation of the hip is pain free.

steps.x: **D. Iliopsoas haematoma.** Deep muscle bleeding is typical of haemophilia: iliopsoas bleed = flexed hip + femoral nerve signs.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with severe haemophilia A on prophylaxis has a sudden severe headache followed by weakness of his left arm and leg. He has not had a head injury. His GCS is 13/15. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 64 bpm and BP 176/98 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Intracranial haemorrhage is the most serious, life-threatening complication of haemophilia and can occur without trauma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: weakness of his left arm and leg
steps.x: Haemophilia, thunderclap-type headache, focal weakness, reduced GCS.

elim: Affects the face only and does not cause limb weakness or headache.
Rare at 52, and a bleed must be assumed in haemophilia.
Possible, but a sudden severe headache with a low GCS in haemophilia means a bleed.
Follows a seizure, which has not happened.

steps.x: **C. Intracranial haemorrhage.** Neurology or headache in haemophilia = intracranial haemorrhage until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man with severe haemophilia A grew up before prophylaxis was available. His left knee has been painful and stiff for 10 years, with crepitus and a fixed flexion deformity. An X-ray shows loss of joint space, subchondral cysts and an enlarged epiphysis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his knee disease?
questions.e: Repeated bleeds into the same joint damage cartilage and synovium, causing chronic haemophilic arthropathy.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Untreated severe haemophilia, one chronically destroyed knee.

elim: Causes acute attacks, usually in the big toe, not a deformed knee from childhood.
Possible chronic monoarthritis, but there are no systemic features and his bleeds explain it.
Polyarticular and symmetrical, not one knee in a haemophiliac.
Acute and febrile, not a 10 year course.

steps.x: **B. Recurrent haemarthroses.** Chronic haemarthrosis = joint damage; prevention is regular prophylactic factor.

questions.stem: A 23 year old man has persistent bleeding from his wound on the second day after an appendicectomy. He has always bruised easily but has never been investigated. His maternal grandfather 'bled a lot'. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Delayed post-surgical bleeding, lifelong easy bruising, a maternal family history and a factor VIII of 22% is mild haemophilia A, which can present late.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Post-surgical bleeding, easy bruising, X-linked family history.

elim: PT, platelets and fibrinogen are normal.
Factor VIII is low, so this is haemophilia A.
The platelet count is normal.
Von Willebrand factor is normal.

steps.x: **D. Mild haemophilia A.** Long APTT + low factor VIII (5 to 40%) = mild haemophilia A, often found after surgery.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy has recently been diagnosed with severe haemophilia A after a swollen ankle. His platelet count is 290 ×10⁹/L (150–400). His parents ask what bleeding to watch for at home.
questions.q: Which pattern of bleeding is he most likely to have?
o: Heavy bleeding from small cuts only
questions.e: Haemophilia causes deep bleeding into joints and muscles, while platelet disorders cause mucocutaneous bleeding such as petechiae, epistaxis and gum bleeding.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
A clotting factor deficiency with normal platelets.

elim: Mucosal bleeding suggests a platelet disorder or von Willebrand disease.
Small cuts usually stop because the platelet plug works.
Petechiae suggest a low platelet count or platelet dysfunction.
Not a typical pattern of haemophilia.

steps.x: **A. Bleeding into joints and muscles.** Factor deficiency = deep bleeds (joints, muscles); platelet disorder = skin and mucosa.

questions.stem: A 2 year old boy has a swollen right knee after a minor fall and several large bruises. His APTT is prolonged and PT normal. His mother is well. The GP is taking a history to decide whether this is an inherited bleeding disorder.
questions.q: Which feature in the history most strongly supports haemophilia?
o: Maternal uncle with a bleeding disorder
questions.e: Haemophilia is X-linked recessive, so it passes through carrier mothers: an affected maternal uncle is the classic family history in a boy.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: APTT is prolonged and PT normal
steps.x: A young boy with a deep bleed and isolated long APTT; the mother is an unaffected likely carrier.

elim: Affected fathers pass the X to daughters, not sons.
Heavy periods are more suggestive of von Willebrand disease.
Suggests immune thrombocytopenia, and his platelets are not described as low.
Mucosal bleeding in a girl suggests von Willebrand disease.

steps.x: **C. Maternal uncle with a bleeding disorder.** Haemophilia risk factors: male, childhood presentation, family history through the mother's side.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy has recurrent bruising and swelling of his left ankle after minor knocks. His coagulation screen shows APTT 68 s (25–35), PT 12 s (10–14) and platelets 301 ×10⁹/L (150–400). His factor VIII assay is 104% (50–150).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: An isolated long APTT with a normal factor VIII excludes haemophilia A, so the factor IX assay is the test that confirms haemophilia B.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.
Haemophilia picture, but factor VIII is normal.

elim: Tests platelet function, which does not explain an isolated long APTT.
The platelet count is normal; this is a clotting factor problem.
Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT, which is normal.
A normal factor VIII already excludes haemophilia A.

steps.x: **C. Factor IX assay.** Normal factor VIII + long APTT = check factor IX (confirms haemophilia B).

questions.stem: A 5 year old boy has a swollen, painful right knee after tripping in the playground. He bruises easily. His mother's brother has haemophilia A. His temperature is 36.8°C. A coagulation screen is sent.
questions.q: Which result is most likely to be abnormal?
questions.e: First-line coagulation screen in haemophilia shows a prolonged APTT with a normal PT and platelet count.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.

clues: His mother's brother has haemophilia A
steps.x: A boy with haemarthrosis and an affected maternal uncle.

elim: Reflects platelet function, which is normal in haemophilia.
Fibrinogen is normal in haemophilia.
Normal in haemophilia.
Tests the extrinsic pathway, which is intact.

steps.x: **A. Activated partial thromboplastin time.** Haemophilia coagulation screen = long APTT, normal PT, normal platelets.

questions.stem: A 9 month old boy has a large swelling on his forehead after a minor bump against a cot rail. He has several bruises on his trunk. His mother's cousin has haemophilia. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: An isolated prolonged APTT in a boy with a family history means a factor deficiency; the factor VIII assay confirms haemophilia A, the commonest type.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.
A boy, a family history on the mother's side, an isolated long APTT.

elim: The problem is an isolated long APTT, not platelets.
Will show the same result and does not identify the factor.
Considered for non-accidental injury, but this clotting screen points to haemophilia.
Worth checking later, but in a boy with this family history factor VIII confirms the commonest cause.

steps.x: **A. Factor VIII assay.** Confirm haemophilia A with a factor VIII assay (factor IX for B).

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy with severe haemophilia A fell off his skateboard and hit his head 2 hours ago. He has a headache and has vomited once. His GCS is 14/15. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. He has just been given recombinant factor VIII in the emergency department.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: A head injury in haemophilia is treated as an intracranial bleed: give factor first, then urgent CT head.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.

clues: has just been given recombinant factor VIII
steps.x: Haemophilia, head injury, headache and vomiting, factor already given.

elim: Useful later, but it must not delay brain imaging.
Contraindicated with a possible bleed and a raised pressure.
Slower and less available; CT is the urgent test for a bleed.
Does not show intracranial bleeding.

steps.x: **A. CT head.** Head injury in haemophilia: factor first, then CT head; never delay factor for the scan.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman's brother has severe haemophilia A. She is planning a pregnancy and wants to know if she is a carrier. Her factor VIII level is 62% (50–150). The family's causative mutation is known.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to determine her carrier status?
o: Genetic testing for the family F8 mutation
questions.e: Haemophilia A is caused by mutations in the F8 gene; carrier status is best shown by testing for the known family mutation.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.
Possible carrier with a normal factor level and a known family mutation.

elim: Usually normal in carriers, so it cannot exclude carriage.
Tests platelet function.
The family has haemophilia A, not B.
Carriers often have normal levels, so a normal level does not exclude carriage.

steps.x: **D. Genetic testing for the family F8 mutation.** Carrier testing for haemophilia A = F8 genetic testing; factor levels can be normal.

questions.stem: A 10 year old boy with severe haemophilia B has a painful, swollen right ankle after landing badly on a trampoline. He cannot bear weight. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. X-ray shows no fracture.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: A joint bleed in haemophilia B needs urgent factor IX replacement, with rest, ice and elevation to protect the joint.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Haemophilia B with an acute haemarthrosis.

elim: Raises factor VIII only and has no role in haemophilia B.
He lacks factor IX, not factor VIII.
Risks more bleeding and infection; replace the factor first.
NSAIDs worsen bleeding, and the bleed needs factor replacement.

steps.x: **B. IV factor IX concentrate.** Haemophilia B bleed = factor IX; haemophilia A bleed = factor VIII.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man with severe haemophilia A (factor VIII below 1%) is listed for an elective knee replacement for haemophilic arthropathy. He has no inhibitors. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to prevent bleeding during surgery?
questions.e: Severe haemophilia A needs factor VIII replacement around surgery; desmopressin is only an adjunct in mild disease.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Severe haemophilia A, major surgery.

elim: Only helps mild haemophilia A; with factor VIII below 1% there is no stored factor to boost.
He has haemophilia A, not B.
Contains too little factor VIII; specific concentrate is used.
His platelets are normal.

steps.x: **C. Factor VIII replacement.** Severe A = factor VIII concentrate; desmopressin only works in mild A.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man with severe haemophilia A is brought in after a car crash. He has a scalp laceration and is drowsy. His GCS is 12/15, pulse rate 58 bpm and BP 168/94 mmHg. His left pupil is larger than the right. A CT scanner is available in 20 minutes.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Wait for the CT head before treatment
questions.e: Suspected intracranial haemorrhage in haemophilia needs urgent recombinant factor replacement before imaging, following UKHCDO guidance.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.

clues: left pupil is larger than the right
steps.x: Head injury, falling GCS, a dilated pupil: an intracranial bleed.

elim: Too weak for severe haemophilia and a life-threatening bleed.
Too little factor VIII; recombinant concentrate is the treatment.
Haemophilia is not a vitamin K problem.
Factor must be given at once; imaging must not delay it.

steps.x: **C. Give recombinant factor VIII now.** Major bleed or suspected ICH in haemophilia = recombinant factor VIII/IX immediately.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy with severe haemophilia B (factor IX below 1%) has had three ankle bleeds and one knee bleed in 4 months, each treated with factor IX when it happened. He is well today. His parents want to stop the bleeds.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
o: Factor IX only when a bleed occurs
questions.e: Long-term management focuses on prevention: regular prophylactic factor replacement (factor IX in haemophilia B) and avoiding trauma.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.

clues: three ankle bleeds and one knee bleed in 4 months
steps.x: Severe haemophilia B with frequent joint bleeds on on-demand treatment.

elim: An antifibrinolytic adjunct that does not replace the missing factor or prevent joint bleeds.
This is what he has now, and it is not preventing joint damage.
He has haemophilia B, not A.
Only for chronic synovitis after failed prophylaxis.

steps.x: **B. Regular prophylactic factor IX.** Severe haemophilia = regular prophylactic factor to prevent joint damage.

questions.stem: An 18 year old man with severe haemophilia A has had factor VIII for a painful knee bleed after football. The swelling is settling. He asks what he can take for the pain at home. He has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate analgesic?
questions.e: After factor replacement, joint protection includes rest, ice and elevation, and analgesia that does not affect platelets: paracetamol, not NSAIDs or aspirin.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
A haemophilia joint bleed being treated: protect the joint and avoid drugs that worsen bleeding.

elim: Inhibits platelets and worsens bleeding.
An NSAID that impairs platelet function.
An NSAID that impairs platelet function.
An NSAID that impairs platelet function.

steps.x: **E. Paracetamol.** Haemophilia analgesia = paracetamol (or opioids); avoid NSAIDs and aspirin.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has haemophilia A. His APTT is 72 s (25–35) but his PT is 12 s (10–14). A medical student asks why only one test is abnormal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Factor VIII acts in the extrinsic pathway only
Factor VIII acts in the intrinsic pathway only
Factor VIII is made by platelets
Low fibrinogen prolongs only the APTT
The PT is insensitive to all factor deficiencies
questions.e: APTT tests the intrinsic pathway, where factors VIII and IX act, so it is prolonged; PT tests the extrinsic pathway, which is intact.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Isolated long APTT in haemophilia A.

elim: Then the PT would be prolonged, not the APTT.
Factor VIII is made mainly in the liver and endothelium; platelets are normal.
Fibrinogen is normal and low fibrinogen prolongs both tests.
PT is prolonged by factor VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen deficiency.

steps.x: **B. Factor VIII acts in the intrinsic pathway only.** Haemophilia: intrinsic pathway fault = long APTT, normal PT.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man with severe haemophilia A has a large thigh haematoma. A student asks which step of clotting fails. His platelet count is normal and a platelet plug forms at injured vessels.
questions.q: Which step of coagulation is most directly impaired?
o: Activation of factor VII by tissue factor
Conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin by plasmin
questions.e: Factor IXa with its cofactor VIIIa activates factor X; without it thrombin generation fails and no stable fibrin clot forms.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Platelets work; a factor VIII (intrinsic pathway) defect.

elim: This is the extrinsic pathway, which is intact.
Plasmin breaks down fibrin; it does not make it.
Platelet function is normal in haemophilia.
This is normal; desmopressin uses it.

steps.x: **B. Activation of factor X.** Factors VIII and IX together activate factor X, the step to thrombin and a stable clot.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man with severe haemophilia A and his unaffected partner are expecting a baby girl. The partner has no family history of bleeding. They ask about the risk to their daughter.
questions.q: Which is the chance that their daughter is a carrier?
questions.e: Haemophilia is X-linked recessive: an affected father passes his X to every daughter (all carriers) and his Y to every son (none affected).

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Affected father, non-carrier mother, a daughter.

elim: She must inherit her father's only X chromosome, which carries the mutation.
This is the risk of an affected child from two autosomal recessive carriers.
This applies to the daughter of a carrier mother, not an affected father.
Not a risk in X-linked inheritance from an affected father.

steps.x: **B. 100%.** Affected father: all daughters carriers, no sons affected.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man with mild haemophilia B (factor IX 20%) needs a tooth extraction. His friend with mild haemophilia A was given desmopressin before his own extraction. He asks why he cannot have the same.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason desmopressin would not help him?
o: It only works in severe haemophilia
It raises factor VIII, not factor IX
questions.e: Desmopressin releases stored von Willebrand factor from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies, which stabilises and transiently raises factor VIII, so it only helps mild haemophilia A.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
A mild deficiency, but of factor IX.

elim: It can be given IV, subcutaneously or intranasally; route is not the reason.
Desmopressin does not lower platelets.
The reverse: it only helps mild haemophilia A.
That is tranexamic acid.

steps.x: **D. It raises factor VIII, not factor IX.** Desmopressin = vWF release = more factor VIII: mild haemophilia A only.

questions.stem: A 12 year old boy with severe haemophilia A cuts his finger on paper. The cut stops bleeding within a few minutes, but the next day he has a knee bleed after a minor twist. His platelets are 260 ×10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the different bleeding?
o: Factor VIII is only found in joints
Skin vessels lack von Willebrand factor
The knee bleed is caused by infection
The platelet plug forms but no stable fibrin clot follows
questions.e: Platelet plugs stop small surface bleeds, but deep tissue bleeding under pressure needs a stable fibrin clot, which haemophilia cannot make; mucocutaneous bleeding suggests a platelet disorder.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.

clues: stops bleeding within a few minutes
knee bleed after a minor twist
steps.x: Surface bleeding stops; deep joint bleeding does not.

elim: Factor VIII circulates in plasma.
His platelets work, which is why the small cut stops.
Skin vessels have vWF; that is why the plug works.
No fever or infection is described.

steps.x: **E. The platelet plug forms but no stable fibrin clot follows.** Haemophilia = deep bleeds (no fibrin); platelet disorders = skin and mucosal bleeds.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man with mild haemophilia A (factor VIII 25%) is given intravenous desmopressin before a minor procedure. An hour later his factor VIII is 60% and his von Willebrand factor has also risen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely source of the von Willebrand factor released?
o: Plasma cells in the bone marrow
questions.e: Desmopressin stimulates release of von Willebrand factor stored in endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies; vWF carries and stabilises factor VIII, so factor VIII rises.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.

clues: von Willebrand factor has also risen
steps.x: Desmopressin causes a rise in vWF and factor VIII.

elim: These store ADP and serotonin, not vWF.
The liver makes factor VIII, but vWF is stored in endothelium and platelets.
Not a store of clotting proteins.
These make antibodies.

steps.x: **E. Weibel-Palade bodies in endothelial cells.** Desmopressin releases vWF from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies.
